winners.premise: A husband charges his wife three hundred dollars for babysitting their son during her hospital stay, although her mother provided the care free.
winners.conflict: A wife must distinguish real household costs from her husband's claim that arranging care makes parenting their own child a paid favor to her.
winners.twist: The grandmother did the actual childcare, while the husband expects payment for organizing it and overlooking the grandmother's need for rest.
winners.hook: My husband charged me three hundred dollars for babysitting our own son while I was in hospital. My mother had done the babysitting.
winners.narration: Dave asked me to transfer it while I was unpacking my hospital bag. I asked whether Mum had charged him. He said the money was for him, because he'd had to arrange everything. I called Mum to thank her and check. She said Leo had stayed with her, free. When I put the phone down, Dave said organizing childcare was work too. I agreed. I'd been doing it around both our jobs for years. Then he said he'd missed a shift driving me to hospital and collecting Leo's things. I said we'd discuss that lost income together. It didn't make looking after our son a service he'd sold me. Mum rang again to ask what time she should collect Leo on Saturday. Dave had already asked her to come back, and she sounded exhausted. I told her we would manage. Dave asked who was supposed to watch him, then. I asked what his plan was. He said I knew the routine better. I pointed at Leo's yellow bag, packed by Mum with his book and clothes. Dave opened it and asked when Leo usually had lunch. I told him, then went to lie down. On Saturday, Mum stayed home. Dave took Leo to the park himself. We still needed to talk about the three hundred dollars. There wasn't another bill for that afternoon.
winners.title: Three Hundred Dollars for Dad's Babysitting
winners.description: He charges his wife for childcare during her hospital stay. The grandmother who actually looked after their son has not charged anyone.
winners.payoff: There wasn't another bill for that afternoon.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF PARENTING IS A SHARED JOB

winners.premise: A mother finds her daughter's prosthetic arm edited out of a school photo and is offered the supposedly normal version for twenty dollars extra.
winners.conflict: A mother must listen to her daughter's view of her own body instead of accepting a photographer's assumption that a different arm makes a better portrait.
winners.twist: The detail the photographer treats as something to remove is the decorated prosthetic cover the child and her grandmother chose together.
winners.hook: I found my daughter's prosthetic arm edited out of her school photo. The photographer wanted twenty dollars extra for what he called the normal version.
winners.narration: The preview showed Ella holding both hands together, except one wasn't the hand she'd posed with. Her blue prosthetic cover was gone too. I asked the photographer whether there'd been a mistake. He said the extra twenty bought the "normal" version, with distractions fixed. Ella asked where her butterflies had gone. She and Grandma had picked the stickers for her cover. I started saying the photo was still lovely, then stopped when she asked whether the other arm was supposed to be better. I told her I should have asked what she thought first. The photographer said children noticed differences more when parents made an issue of them. I asked to see the picture he'd actually taken. He brought up the original and called it uncorrected. Ella pointed straight at it. She said that was the one Grandma would recognize. He asked whether I really wanted to pay for the basic version when he'd spent time on the other one. I said we wanted the photograph Ella had chosen. She asked whether she could take it to Grandma before we framed it. I said yes. On the way home, she counted the butterflies in the picture to check they were all there. Grandma had helped her pick seven. None of them needed correcting.
winners.title: Seven Butterflies in Her School Portrait
winners.description: The photographer calls the edited portrait an upgrade. The girl in the picture wants to know why the details she chose have disappeared.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF HER CHOICE BELONGS IN THE PICTURE

winners.premise: A boss admits disguising a loan application as his mother's holiday booking and asks an employee translating it to omit that her house is security.
winners.conflict: An employee must translate honestly when her boss wants her credibility to obtain his mother's signature without explaining the risk to her home.
winners.twist: The mother requested someone else read the form precisely because she wanted to understand the supposed gift before signing anything.
winners.hook: My boss admitted disguising a loan application as his mother's holiday booking. He told me not to translate the line putting her house up as security.
winners.narration: Gary pointed out the page to skip before his mother's birthday lunch. She'd asked someone else to read the English paperwork in her language. He said his business needed money, and the details would only worry her. I asked whether she knew there was a loan. He said she thought she was signing for the promised trip. Then he reminded me who paid my wages. His mother came in carrying a new blue suitcase and asked what time the flight left. Gary said we'd get to that after the forms. She handed me the paperwork and asked me to read it from the beginning. I translated the application as it was written, including the part naming her home as security. Gary interrupted and said I was making it sound frightening. She asked him whether it was true. He said the business would recover before she needed to worry. She put the pen down. Then she asked where the holiday was booked. He admitted there wasn't a booking yet. I didn't offer to explain that part for him. She moved the suitcase back beside her chair and told him to sit down. She wanted to hear what was happening with the business, without another promise about a trip. The loan form stayed unsigned. He had to do the talking himself.
winners.title: His Mother's Holiday Booking
winners.description: His mother asks for the holiday paperwork to be translated before she signs. Her son wants one important section left unread.
winners.payoff: He had to do the talking himself.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF EVERY LINE DESERVES THE TRUTH

winners.premise: A landlord installs a clear glass front door to see into his tenant's living room and tells her she cannot cover it.
winners.conflict: A tenant must protect privacy in her own home when the landlord treats owning the door as permission to keep a view into her living space.
winners.twist: The landlord rejects even a curtain that needs no drilling, revealing that the view matters more to him than preventing damage to the frame.
winners.hook: My landlord installed a clear glass front door so he could see into my living room. He said I wasn't allowed to cover it.
winners.narration: Peter replaced the damaged door while I was out. When I came home, my sofa and dinner table were visible from the corridor. He said it would help him check the property and see who visited. I asked when I was supposed to have privacy. He said I could close the bedroom door if I needed it. I said I'd buy a curtain. He told me drilling into the new frame would be damage, so I offered to use a curtain that didn't need any holes. He said covering the glass defeated the point. That was when I stopped discussing how to attach something to his door. I bought a freestanding screen and put it inside my living room, leaving the entrance clear. Next time he came, he complained he couldn't see behind it. I said the lock worked, the door opened, and nothing had been attached to the frame. He asked what I was trying to hide. I told him I wanted to eat dinner without someone inspecting it from the corridor. He said we still needed to discuss the arrangement. I said we could arrange a time to talk. Then I went back inside and left the screen where it was. When he wanted another answer, he had to knock. I decided when to open the door.
winners.title: The View Through Her Front Door
winners.description: A new glass door gives the landlord the view he wants. His tenant has a different idea about what access to her home should mean.
winners.payoff: I decided when to open the door.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF RENTING STILL MEANS PRIVACY
